titre: Steno, 1669: A Shark's Head Opens the Layers of Time
accroche: In 1666, a shark's head dissected in Florence leads Nicolas Steno to ask how one solid forms inside another solid.
contenu_vulgarise:
In October 1666, two fishermen from Livorno haul in a large female shark. The Grand Duke of Tuscany, Ferdinand II de' Medici, has the head brought to his personal physician: Nicolas Steno, a Dane recently settled in Florence. Steno opens the jaws, counts the rows of teeth, and notices a troubling resemblance to “glossopetrae,” tongue-shaped stones found in the Tuscan hills that people have believed, since antiquity, grew directly inside the rock, like a crystal.

## A solid inside another solid

If the glossopetrae are in fact fossil teeth, something must explain how a once-soft tissue ended up mineral, inside a rock that is itself solid. Steno publishes the answer in 1669 in Florence, in a text with a modest title: *De solido intra solidum naturaliter contento dissertationis prodromus* (“Preliminary Discourse to a Dissertation on a Solid Naturally Contained within a Solid”). His general rule: when the contact surfaces between two bodies match exactly, one of them must have still been fluid when it took the shape of the other, and is therefore younger. A tooth embedded in stone hardened after the stone that encloses it, not before.

## Strata as chronology

Steno then applies this reasoning to rock layers themselves. He writes that at the time an upper stratum was forming, the lower stratum had already gained the consistency of a solid: the lowest layer is therefore the oldest. He adds that a layer is deposited horizontally, parallel to the horizon “so far as possible,” and that it extends sideways until it meets another solid that stops it. Three rules, written down for the first time in this order, turn a stack of rocks into a datable sequence: bottom before top, horizontal before tilted, continuous before broken.

## What this shifts

Steno dates no stratum in years: he only gives them an order. But it is this order that makes it thinkable, more than a century later, that a pile of rocks tells a history rather than a frozen state. William Smith will use fossils to tell apart, in 1815, layers identical in appearance; nineteenth-century geologists will stack geological eras on this same principle of superposition. It all starts with a shark's head laid on a Danish physician's table, and a question that could have remained a passing anatomical curiosity.

carte.punch: A dissected shark's head in 1666 invents the rule that dates every rock on Earth.
carte.idee: In 1669, Nicolas Steno proposed that, in a stack of rocks, the bottom layer formed before the one above it, and that a layer is deposited horizontally before it tilts. Born from a fossil shark's tooth, this rule lets geologists read strata as a timeline.

quiz.question: Why does Steno conclude that a tooth embedded in rock is younger than the rock enclosing it?
choix: Because teeth are always smaller than the rock that contains them
Because the two contact surfaces match exactly, a sign that one was soft when it took the other's shape
Because glossopetrae are mentioned in texts older than the rock that holds them
Because the Grand Duke of Tuscany had already dated the rock by another method
quiz.explication: Steno sets out a general rule: when two contact surfaces fit exactly, the body that took the other's shape was still soft at that moment, and is therefore more recent. None of the other claims appear anywhere in his reasoning.
